reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze and pump blood.
expectation: The muscle will surround the chambers so they can contract.

effect: The chambers can squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so they need a way to direct flow.
reaction: The two-way flow makes the need for valves clear.
reason: The valves are shown closing against reverse flow, which should help the pump move blood forward.
expectation: The valves will prevent backward flow through the chambers.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and refill; the pump still needs repeated contractions.
reaction: The paired squeeze and refill panels make the valves’ roles clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells produce a spreading electrical wave, suggesting they can coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will give the heart a repeating contraction signal.

effect: The heart now beats with coordinated contractions, completing the pump goal. It still needs blood and a returning route.
reaction: The distinction between starting a beat and nerves adjusting its rhythm is useful.
reason: Hemoglobin has oxygen-binding sites, and the red-cell envelopes provide a place to carry it.
expectation: The envelopes will become oxygen-carrying red cells.

effect: The red blood cells carry hemoglobin and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria; they can now be combined with plasma to make blood.
reaction: The different way these cells make ATP is interesting alongside the earlier muscle-cell model.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The cells and plasma will form blood for the returning route.

effect: The red cells and plasma form oxygen-carrying blood, ready to be fitted into a circulation route.
reaction: The inset helps show that blood includes more than red cells and plasma.
reason: Arteries and veins carry blood away from and back toward the heart, while capillaries can connect their branches.
expectation: The capillary networks will connect the arteries and veins into a returning vessel route.

effect: The capillaries connect the arteries and veins into a circuit with slots for a pump and transport medium.
reaction: The named slots make the remaining fittings clear.
reason: The beating heart can fill the circuit’s pump slot.
expectation: The heart will be fitted into the circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart is fitted into the vessel circuit; the transport medium slot remains.
reaction: The heart’s connections to outgoing and returning vessels are clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood is the available transport medium for the circuit.
expectation: The blood will fill the transport medium slot and complete the circulating route.

effect: The blood completes the circuit. The exchange inset shows oxygen and nutrients reaching tissue while carbon dioxide returns, connecting circulation to cellular work.
reaction: Seeing the closed route and tissue exchange together is satisfying, though the exchange depends on the blood being supplied.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding valves was worthwhile because the before-and-after pictures explain how squeezing can drive flow forward instead of toward both openings.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart into its named slot was straightforward, but the result added little beyond confirming the connection.

surprise.text: The red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria, unlike the muscle cells encountered earlier.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures and named slots gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would continue: the chapter made the pump and returning route understandable, and I would be curious to see how the body supplies the blood with oxygen.
